notes:
1. Early Resistance to British Rule

  • Resistance to British expansion began long before the establishment of the Indian National Congress in 1885.
  • Early resistance took several forms:
  • Local ruler rebellions.
  • Palayakkarar resistance.
  • Tribal uprisings.
  • Peasant revolts.
  • Military mutinies.
  • Religious-political movements.
  • The Revolt of 1857 became the largest anti-British uprising of the nineteenth century.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Early Resistance → Local Revolts → Tribal/Peasant Resistance → Military Mutinies → Revolt of 1857

2. Causes of Early Uprisings

  • Common causes included:
  • British territorial expansion.
  • Heavy land revenue.
  • Loss of hereditary rights.
  • Interference with local rulers.
  • Destruction of traditional political authority.
  • Exploitation by moneylenders and zamindars.
  • Changes in military service.
  • Religious and social fears.

3. Nature of Early Revolts

  • Most early uprisings were regional rather than all-India movements.
  • Their objectives differed according to local circumstances.
  • They nevertheless weakened the belief that British expansion faced no resistance.

4. Sanyasi–Fakir Rebellion

  • The Sanyasi and Fakir uprisings occurred mainly in Bengal during the late eighteenth century.
  • They developed after the East India Company acquired Diwani rights in Bengal in 1765.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sanyasi–Fakir Rebellion → Bengal

5. Background of Sanyasi Resistance

  • Factors included:
  • Severe revenue demands.
  • Bengal famine.
  • Restrictions on movement and religious practices.
  • Decline of traditional patronage.

6. Fakir Resistance

  • Muslim fakirs also participated in resistance against Company authority.
  • Majnu Shah became an important Fakir leader.
📌 Must-Memorise

Majnu Shah → Fakir Rebellion

7. Sanyasi Rebellion in Literature

  • Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay later used the Sanyasi rebellion as background for his novel Anandamath.
📌 Must-Memorise

Anandamath → Sanyasi Rebellion Background

8. Vande Mataram

  • Vande Mataram appeared in Bankim Chandra's Anandamath.
  • It later became an important nationalist song.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anandamath → Bankim Chandra → Vande Mataram

9. Chuar Uprisings

  • Chuar uprisings occurred in the Jungle Mahal areas of Bengal.
  • Important centres included:
  • Midnapore.
  • Bankura.
  • Several phases occurred during the late eighteenth century.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chuar Rebellion → Jungle Mahal → Bengal

10. Causes of Chuar Revolt

  • Important causes included:
  • Increased revenue demand.
  • Loss of land.
  • Displacement of local chiefs.
  • Economic hardship.

11. Durjan Singh

  • Durjan Singh was one of the leaders associated with the Chuar resistance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Durjan Singh → Chuar Uprising

12. Palayakkarar Resistance in Tamil Nadu

  • Some of the earliest organised armed resistance to British expansion in South India came from Tamil Palayakkarars.
  • Palayakkarars controlled local military-revenue territories called Palayams.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Palayam → Palayakkarar / Polygar

13. Meaning of Polygar

  • "Polygar" was the English rendering of the Tamil term Palayakkarar.
  • Palayakkarars maintained:
  • Armed forces.
  • Forts.
  • Revenue administration.

14. Puli Thevar

  • Puli Thevar was one of the earliest Tamil rulers to resist the expansion of the English East India Company and its allies.
  • He ruled from Nerkattumseval.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Puli Thevar → Nerkattumseval

15. Puli Thevar's Resistance

  • His major resistance occurred during the 1750s and 1760s.
  • He opposed revenue demands connected with the Nawab of Arcot and the East India Company.

16. Significance of Puli Thevar

  • Puli Thevar attempted to organise alliances among western Palayakkarars.
  • His resistance preceded the better-known Kattabomman uprising.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Puli Thevar Resistance → Earlier Than Kattabomman

17. Nerkattumseval

  • Nerkattumseval is located in present-day Tenkasi district region.
  • It was Puli Thevar's principal stronghold.

18. Nawab of Arcot

  • The Nawab of Arcot became financially dependent on the East India Company.
  • Company attempts to collect revenue from Palayakkarars intensified local resistance.

19. Velu Nachiyar

  • Rani Velu Nachiyar was queen of Sivaganga.
  • She became one of the earliest Indian queens to wage armed resistance against the East India Company's allies.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Velu Nachiyar → Sivaganga

20. Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar

  • Velu Nachiyar's husband, Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar, was killed during conflict with forces connected to the Nawab of Arcot and the Company.

21. Velu Nachiyar in Exile

  • Velu Nachiyar escaped from Sivaganga.
  • She reorganised resistance with the support of allies.

22. Hyder Ali and Velu Nachiyar

  • Velu Nachiyar obtained support from Hyder Ali of Mysore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Velu Nachiyar → Allied with Hyder Ali

23. Marudhu Brothers and Velu Nachiyar

  • Periya Marudhu and Chinna Marudhu became important military supporters of Velu Nachiyar.

24. Kuyili

  • Kuyili was a woman commander associated with Velu Nachiyar.
  • Tamil tradition remembers her for a self-sacrificing attack on an enemy ammunition store.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kuyili → Velu Nachiyar's Commander

25. Recovery of Sivaganga

  • Velu Nachiyar recovered control over Sivaganga around 1780.
  • She subsequently ruled the region for several years.

26. Veerapandiya Kattabomman

  • Veerapandiya Kattabomman was the Palayakkarar of Panchalankurichi.
  • He became one of Tamil Nadu's most famous early anti-British resistance leaders.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kattabomman → Panchalankurichi

27. Panchalankurichi

  • Panchalankurichi was Kattabomman's fortified Palayam.
  • It is located in present-day Thoothukudi district.

28. Cause of Kattabomman's Conflict

  • The main immediate dispute concerned tribute/revenue demanded by the East India Company.
  • Kattabomman resisted increasing Company interference.

29. Collector Jackson

  • Collector Jackson became involved in a serious confrontation with Kattabomman.
  • His handling of the issue increased tensions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Collector Jackson → Kattabomman Conflict

30. Ramanathapuram Meeting

  • Kattabomman met Collector Jackson at Ramanathapuram.
  • The meeting ended in conflict and distrust.

31. First Polygar War

  • Kattabomman's conflict with the Company culminated in the First Polygar War of 1799.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Polygar War → 1799

32. Major Bannerman

  • Major John Bannerman led Company operations against Kattabomman.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bannerman → Campaign Against Kattabomman

33. Fall of Panchalankurichi

  • Company forces attacked Panchalankurichi.
  • Kattabomman escaped temporarily.

34. Capture of Kattabomman

  • Kattabomman was eventually captured after seeking refuge away from Panchalankurichi.
  • He was handed over to British authorities.

35. Execution of Kattabomman

  • Veerapandiya Kattabomman was executed at Kayathar on 16 October 1799.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kattabomman → Kayathar → 16 October 1799

36. Oomathurai

  • Oomathurai was Kattabomman's brother.
  • He continued resistance after Kattabomman's execution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Oomathurai → Brother of Kattabomman

37. Second Polygar War

  • A larger rebellion erupted in 1800–1801.
  • It is called:
  • Second Polygar War.
  • South Indian Rebellion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Polygar War / South Indian Rebellion → 1800–1801

38. Marudhu Brothers

  • The two major leaders were:
  • Periya Marudhu.
  • Chinna Marudhu.
  • They were associated with Sivaganga.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Marudhu Brothers → Sivaganga

39. South Indian Confederacy

  • Resistance leaders attempted to create a broader alliance against British power.
  • Support came from various Palayakkarars and regional chiefs.

40. Jambudweep Proclamation

  • The Marudhu Brothers issued a famous anti-British proclamation in 1801.
  • It called upon different sections of the population to unite against foreign rule.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Jambudweep Proclamation → Marudhu Brothers → 1801

41. Importance of Jambudweep Proclamation

  • It is regarded as one of the earliest proclamations calling for broad resistance to British authority in India.

42. Tiruchirappalli–Srirangam Connection

  • Copies of the proclamation were associated with public circulation around places such as Tiruchirappalli and Srirangam.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1801 Proclamation → Tiruchirappalli/Srirangam Region

43. Sivaganga Resistance

  • The Marudhu Brothers made Sivaganga an important centre of rebellion.
  • Company forces launched extensive operations against them.

44. Capture of Marudhu Brothers

  • British forces eventually defeated the Sivaganga resistance.
  • The Marudhu Brothers were captured.

45. Execution of Marudhu Brothers

  • Periya Marudhu and Chinna Marudhu were executed at Tirupattur on 24 October 1801.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Marudhu Brothers → Tirupattur → 24 October 1801

46. Oomathurai's Later Resistance

  • Oomathurai escaped imprisonment and helped revive resistance at Panchalankurichi.
  • He later joined wider rebel operations.

47. Oomathurai's Death

  • Oomathurai was eventually captured and executed by the Company in 1801.

48. Dheeran Chinnamalai

  • Dheeran Chinnamalai was a major resistance leader from Kongu Nadu.
  • His original name was Theerthagiri.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Dheeran Chinnamalai → Theerthagiri → Kongu Nadu

49. Odanilai

  • Odanilai became an important stronghold associated with Dheeran Chinnamalai.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Odanilai → Dheeran Chinnamalai

50. Dheeran Chinnamalai's Resistance

  • He fought Company forces in the western Tamil region.
  • His campaigns were part of the wider South Indian resistance.

51. Sankagiri

  • Dheeran Chinnamalai was captured and executed at Sankagiri Fort in 1805.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Dheeran Chinnamalai → Sankagiri → 1805

52. Importance of the Polygar Resistance

  • The Palayakkarar uprisings demonstrated:
  • Early armed resistance.
  • Opposition to revenue control.
  • Defence of regional autonomy.
  • Attempts at military confederacy.

53. British Response to Polygar Resistance

  • After suppressing the uprisings, the British:
  • Destroyed or reduced several forts.
  • Confiscated arms.
  • Strengthened revenue administration.
  • Reduced independent military power of Palayakkarars.

54. Vellore Mutiny

  • Vellore Mutiny took place on 10 July 1806.
  • It was the first major sepoy mutiny against the British before 1857.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Vellore Mutiny → 10 July 1806

55. Location

  • The uprising occurred at Vellore Fort in Tamil Nadu.

56. Causes of Vellore Mutiny

  • Sepoys opposed new military regulations involving:
  • Headgear.
  • Dress.
  • Religious symbols.
  • Caste marks.
  • Facial-hair regulations.

57. Religious Fear

  • Hindu soldiers feared interference with caste practices.
  • Muslim soldiers also objected to aspects of the new dress regulations.
  • Rumours of forced conversion increased suspicion.

58. Tipu Sultan's Family

  • Members of Tipu Sultan's family were confined at Vellore Fort after the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.
  • Their presence contributed to the political atmosphere of the mutiny.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vellore Fort → Tipu Sultan's Family

59. Outbreak

  • Indian soldiers attacked British officers and troops inside the fort.
  • The rebels briefly took control of Vellore Fort.

60. Mysore Flag

  • The rebels reportedly raised a flag associated with the Mysore royal family and attempted to restore Tipu Sultan's lineage.

61. Rollo Gillespie

  • Colonel Rollo Gillespie rushed from Arcot with troops and suppressed the mutiny.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vellore Mutiny Suppressed by → Rollo Gillespie

62. Suppression

  • The mutiny was suppressed within hours.
  • Large numbers of Indian soldiers were killed or punished.

63. Consequences of Vellore Mutiny

  • The British:
  • Withdrew the unpopular dress regulations.
  • Punished officials.
  • Reassessed military policy.

64. William Bentinck and Vellore

  • Lord William Bentinck was Governor of Madras during the Vellore Mutiny.
  • He was recalled following the crisis.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

William Bentinck → Governor of Madras During Vellore Mutiny

Later → Governor-General Associated with Sati Abolition

65. Vellore vs 1857

  • Vellore:
  • -
  • 1806.
  • 1) Tamil Nadu.
  • 2) Military revolt.
  • 3) Tipu family connection.
  • 1857:
  • Northern and central India.
  • Much larger territorial scale.

66. Paika Rebellion

  • The Paika Rebellion occurred in Odisha in 1817.
  • It was led by Bakshi Jagabandhu.
📌 Must-Memorise

Paika Rebellion → 1817 → Bakshi Jagabandhu

67. Paikas

  • Paikas were traditional landed militia in Odisha.
  • They performed military service for the Khurda rulers.

68. Causes of Paika Rebellion

  • Important causes included:
  • British conquest of Odisha.
  • Loss of rent-free lands.
  • Revenue changes.
  • Decline of traditional privileges.
  • Economic hardship.

69. Khurda

  • Khurda was the main geographical centre of the Paika resistance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Paika → Khurda → Odisha

70. Bakshi Jagabandhu

  • Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar was hereditary military commander of the Khurda kingdom.
  • Loss of his estates contributed to his opposition.

71. Wider Participation

  • The rebellion involved:
  • Paikas.
  • Peasants.
  • Local chiefs.
  • Tribal communities.

72. British Suppression

  • British troops eventually suppressed the main uprising.
  • Jagabandhu continued resistance for some years before surrendering.

73. Kittur Rebellion

  • Kittur resistance occurred in Karnataka in 1824.
  • It was led by Rani Chennamma.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kittur → 1824 → Rani Chennamma

74. Rani Chennamma

  • Rani Chennamma was queen of Kittur.
  • She opposed British refusal to recognise an adopted heir.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rani Chennamma → Kittur

75. Succession Dispute at Kittur

  • After the death of Kittur's ruler, an adopted heir was nominated.
  • British authorities refused to accept the succession and attempted to take control.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Kittur Dispute → Before Formal Doctrine of Lapse under Dalhousie

76. British Officer St. John Thackeray

  • British official St. John Thackeray was killed during the fighting at Kittur.

77. Capture of Rani Chennamma

  • British reinforcements eventually defeated Kittur.
  • Rani Chennamma was imprisoned.

78. Sangolli Rayanna

  • Sangolli Rayanna continued resistance after Rani Chennamma's defeat.
  • He used guerrilla tactics against British forces.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sangolli Rayanna → Kittur Resistance

79. Execution of Sangolli Rayanna

  • Sangolli Rayanna was captured and executed in 1831.

80. Ramosi Uprisings

  • Ramosi communities of western India rebelled against British authority during the early nineteenth century.
  • Maharashtra was an important centre.

81. Umaji Naik

  • Umaji Naik became one of the best-known Ramosi resistance leaders.
📌 Must-Memorise

Umaji Naik → Ramosi Resistance

82. Causes of Ramosi Resistance

  • Factors included:
  • Loss of traditional employment.
  • British administrative changes.
  • Economic hardship.
  • Displacement of local warrior communities.

83. Bhil Uprisings

  • Bhil communities resisted British authority in western and central India.
  • Important regions included Khandesh and adjoining areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhil Uprisings → Western/Central India

84. Causes of Bhil Revolts

  • Loss of forest access.
  • Administrative interference.
  • Revenue pressures.
  • Political displacement.

85. Ahom Revolt

  • Ahom resistance developed in Assam after the First Anglo-Burmese War.
  • The British had promised restoration of Ahom authority but retained political control.

86. Gomdhar Konwar

  • Gomdhar Konwar led an Ahom uprising in 1828.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ahom Revolt → 1828 → Gomdhar Konwar

87. Assam

  • The Ahom revolt reflected regional resentment against British occupation of Assam.

88. Khasi Uprising

  • Khasi resistance occurred in the northeastern hills from 1829 to 1833.
  • Tirot Sing was its most famous leader.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khasi Uprising → Tirot Sing

89. Cause of Khasi Resistance

  • British plans to construct roads through Khasi territory threatened local political autonomy.

90. Tirot Sing

  • Tirot Sing organised resistance against British expansion into the Khasi Hills.

91. Khasi Guerrilla Warfare

  • Khasi forces used difficult hill terrain for guerrilla resistance.
  • The British eventually suppressed the uprising.

92. Kol Uprising

  • The Kol uprising occurred in Chotanagpur during 1831–1832.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kol Uprising → 1831–32 → Chotanagpur

93. Causes of Kol Uprising

  • Important causes included:
  • Land alienation.
  • Entry of outsiders.
  • Moneylenders.
  • Revenue farmers.
  • Breakdown of traditional tribal authority.

94. Buddhu Bhagat

  • Buddhu Bhagat was an important leader associated with tribal resistance in the Chotanagpur region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Buddhu Bhagat → Kol-Region Resistance

95. Santhal Rebellion

  • The Santhal uprising occurred in 1855–1856.
  • It is also called the Santhal Hul.
📌 Must-Memorise

Santhal Hul → 1855–56

96. Santhal Leaders

  • Major leaders included:
  • Sidhu Murmu.
  • Kanhu Murmu.
  • Chand Murmu.
  • Bhairav Murmu.
📌 Must-Memorise

Santhal → Sidhu + Kanhu

97. Santhal Homeland

  • The rebellion spread through areas around:
  • Rajmahal Hills.
  • Present Jharkhand.
  • Parts of Bengal region.

98. Damin-i-Koh

  • Damin-i-Koh was an area where Santhals had been encouraged by colonial authorities to settle and cultivate.
📌 Must-Memorise

Damin-i-Koh → Santhal Settlement Zone

99. Causes of Santhal Rebellion

  • Santhals opposed exploitation by:
  • Zamindars.
  • Moneylenders.
  • Revenue officials.
  • Police.
  • Colonial authorities.

100. Dikus

  • Santhals used the term Diku for exploitative outsiders.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diku → Outsider in Santhal Context

101. Beginning of Santhal Hul

  • Sidhu and Kanhu called for rebellion at Bhognadih in 1855.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhognadih → Santhal Hul

102. Suppression of Santhal Rebellion

  • British forces used extensive military power to suppress the revolt.
  • Thousands of Santhals were killed.

103. Administrative Consequence

  • The uprising contributed to the creation of a separate administrative arrangement for the Santhal Parganas.

104. Faraizi Movement

  • The Faraizi Movement began in Bengal.
  • Haji Shariatullah was its founder.
📌 Must-Memorise

Faraizi Movement → Haji Shariatullah

105. Meaning of Faraizi

  • The movement emphasised performance of the obligatory duties of Islam.

106. Dudu Miyan

  • Dudu Miyan, son of Haji Shariatullah, expanded the movement.
  • Under him it developed a strong agrarian character.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dudu Miyan → Faraizi Agrarian Resistance

107. Faraizi Social Base

  • The movement gained support among:
  • Muslim peasants.
  • Rural tenants.
  • Cultivators.

108. Wahabi Movement in India

  • Reformist Islamic networks associated with Sayyid Ahmad Barelvi influenced resistance movements in the nineteenth century.
  • Later Wahabi networks opposed British authority.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sayyid Ahmad Barelvi → Wahabi/Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya Movement

109. Patna

  • Patna became an important centre of Wahabi activity in India.

110. British Suppression of Wahabis

  • British authorities prosecuted suspected Wahabi leaders in a series of trials during the nineteenth century.

111. Mappila Uprisings

  • Mappila peasant uprisings occurred repeatedly in Malabar during the nineteenth century.
  • They had both:
  • Agrarian.
  • Religious-social dimensions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mappila Uprisings → Malabar

112. Agrarian Context of Mappila Resistance

  • Causes included:
  • Tenant grievances.
  • Landlord power.
  • Revenue pressure.
  • Colonial legal arrangements.

113. Mappila Rebellion of 1921 — Distinction

  • The major Malabar/Mappila rebellion of 1921 belonged to a later nationalist-era context.
  • It should not be confused with the earlier nineteenth-century outbreaks.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mappila Uprisings → Multiple Phases; 1921 Is Later

114. Indigo Revolt

  • Indigo cultivators in Bengal rebelled against European indigo planters in 1859–1860.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indigo Revolt → 1859–60 → Bengal

115. Cause of Indigo Revolt

  • Peasants were often forced to cultivate indigo under:
  • Unfavourable contracts.
  • Low payments.
  • Coercion by planters.

116. Indigo Cultivation

  • Indigo was a commercial dye crop.
  • Cultivation often reduced cultivators' ability to produce food crops profitably.

117. Nil Darpan

  • Dinabandhu Mitra wrote the play Nil Darpan exposing exploitation of indigo cultivators.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nil Darpan → Dinabandhu Mitra → Indigo Exploitation

118. Indigo Commission

  • The colonial government appointed the Indigo Commission in 1860.
  • It investigated planter abuses.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indigo Commission → 1860

119. Pabna Agrarian Unrest

  • Agrarian movements occurred in Pabna in Bengal during the 1870s.
  • Peasants resisted illegal rent increases and zamindar oppression.

120. Pabna Agrarian Leagues

  • Peasants formed associations to challenge landlords through organised and often legal methods.

121. Deccan Riots

  • Deccan Riots occurred in western India in 1875.
  • Peasants attacked moneylenders and destroyed debt records.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deccan Riots → 1875 → Maharashtra

122. Causes of Deccan Riots

  • Important causes included:
  • Heavy debt.
  • High revenue.
  • Falling agricultural prices.
  • Moneylender exploitation.

123. Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act

  • The British passed the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act in 1879.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act → 1879

124. Revolt of 1857 — Overview

  • The Revolt of 1857 was the largest armed uprising against British rule in nineteenth-century India.
  • It began as a sepoy revolt and expanded into a wider political and popular rebellion in several regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Revolt of 1857 → Began at Meerut → 10 May 1857

125. Different Names for Revolt of 1857

  • It has been called:
  • Sepoy Mutiny.
  • Revolt of 1857.
  • Great Revolt.
  • First War of Indian Independence.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Different Historians Use Different Interpretations

126. V.D. Savarkar

  • V.D. Savarkar popularised the interpretation of 1857 as the "First War of Indian Independence."
📌 Must-Memorise

First War of Indian Independence Interpretation → V.D. Savarkar

127. Immediate Military Cause

  • The immediate trigger was controversy over the new Enfield rifle cartridges.

128. Enfield Rifle

  • Soldiers were required to bite open cartridges before loading.
  • A rumour spread that cartridge grease contained:
  • Cow fat.
  • Pig fat.
📌 Must-Memorise

1857 Immediate Cause → Enfield Cartridge Controversy

129. Religious Sensitivities

  • Cow fat offended Hindu religious sentiment.
  • Pig fat offended Muslim religious sentiment.

130. General Military Grievances

  • Sepoys also resented:
  • Low pay compared with Europeans.
  • Racial discrimination.
  • Limited promotion.
  • Overseas-service fears.
  • Changes in allowances.

131. General Service Enlistment Act

  • The General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 increased fears that soldiers might be compelled to serve overseas.
📌 Must-Memorise

General Service Enlistment Act → 1856

132. Political Causes of 1857

  • Important causes included:
  • Doctrine of Lapse.
  • Annexation of Awadh.
  • Removal of rulers.
  • Loss of aristocratic privileges.

133. Doctrine of Lapse

  • Lord Dalhousie used the Doctrine of Lapse to annex states where an adopted heir was not recognised as successor under Company policy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Doctrine of Lapse → Lord Dalhousie

134. States Annexed under Doctrine of Lapse

  • Important examples included:
  • Satara.
  • Jhansi.
  • Nagpur.

135. Jhansi

  • British refusal to recognise the adopted heir of Jhansi became a major grievance of Rani Lakshmibai.

136. Annexation of Awadh

  • Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of alleged misgovernment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Awadh Annexed → 1856

137. Why Awadh Annexation Mattered

  • Many Bengal Army sepoys came from Awadh.
  • Annexation affected:
  • Soldiers.
  • Talukdars.
  • Court elites.
  • Peasants.

138. Economic Causes of 1857

  • Discontent arose from:
  • Heavy revenue.
  • Land dispossession.
  • Decline of aristocratic patronage.
  • Handicraft decline.
  • Rural debt.

139. Social-Religious Fears

  • British policies created fears of:
  • Religious conversion.
  • Interference in customs.
  • Destruction of caste.
  • Christian missionary expansion.

140. Social Reform and Misinterpretation

  • Measures such as the Widow Remarriage Act were themselves reform laws.
  • But sections of society interpreted British social legislation as evidence of broader interference.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Reform Legislation ≠ Cause by Itself; Fear of Interference Was Politically Important

141. Mangal Pandey

  • Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry.
  • He attacked British officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mangal Pandey → Barrackpore → 29 March 1857

142. Execution of Mangal Pandey

  • Mangal Pandey was executed on 8 April 1857.

143. Meerut

  • The main outbreak began at Meerut on 10 May 1857.
📌 Must-Memorise

Meerut → 10 May 1857

144. 85 Sepoys

  • Eighty-five cavalrymen who refused to use the cartridges were court-martialled and imprisoned at Meerut.
  • Their punishment triggered greater anger.

145. Revolt at Meerut

  • Sepoys released imprisoned soldiers.
  • They attacked British officers and moved toward Delhi.

146. Delhi

  • Rebels entered Delhi on 11 May 1857.
  • Bahadur Shah II was proclaimed symbolic emperor.
📌 Must-Memorise

Delhi → Bahadur Shah Zafar

180. Reasons for Failure of 1857

  • Important reasons included:
  • Limited geographical spread.
  • Lack of unified command.
  • Different aims among leaders.
  • Weak coordination.
  • British control of communication.
  • British military resources.
  • Support received by British from several Indian rulers and groups.

181. Lack of Common Programme

  • Different groups fought for:
  • Restoration of old rulers.
  • Local rights.
  • Land.
  • Military grievances.
  • Religious concerns.
  • There was no single modern national programme.

  • The British used:
  • Telegraph.
  • Postal networks.
  • Roads.
  • Railways where available.
  • to coordinate military response.

183. Modern Weapons

  • British forces had stronger access to modern arms and reinforcements.

184. Indian Princes
